title: Heritage sites in Jammu and Kashmir: Martand, Burzahom and Srinagar

summary: Jammu and Kashmir has no UNESCO cultural site, but its heritage is deep. Burzahom has Neolithic pit dwellings, Harwan has stamped terracotta tiles from a Buddhist site, and Martand, Avantipora and Pandrethan preserve Kashmir's stone temple style. Srinagar adds wooden shrines such as Khanqah-e-Maula, the Jamia Masjid and the Mughal gardens, while Jammu has Akhnoor and the Babor temples.

paras: The Kashmir valley was settled by Neolithic farmers by about the 3rd millennium BCE. It became a centre of Buddhism under the Kushans, and Kalhana's Rajatarangini, written in the 12th century, records a long line of kings. The Karkota and Utpala rulers of the 8th and 9th centuries built the great stone temples. From the 14th century Sultans ruled, followed by the Mughals, Afghans, Sikhs and the Dogra dynasty of Jammu.

Kashmir was also a centre of Sanskrit learning and Shaiva philosophy, and it developed its own script, Sharada. Our course [Reading Śāradā script](sarada-script.html) and the explainer on [ancient scripts of India](ancient-scripts-of-india.html) introduce it.

sections.h2: Burzahom and Harwan: archaeology of the valley
paras: Burzahom, north-east of Srinagar, is the key Neolithic site of Kashmir. Excavations found pit dwellings dug into the loess, bone and stone tools, burials with dogs, and a stone slab engraved with a hunting scene and two suns. Later phases had mud-brick houses and megaliths. Our lecture [From stone tools to the first villages](from-stone-tools-to-the-first-villages.html) places Burzahom among India's early farming sites.

Harwan, near the Shalimar garden, is a Buddhist site of about the early centuries CE with terraced structures and a famous floor of moulded terracotta tiles showing dancers, animals and figures in Central Asian dress. Parihaspora, near Pattan, has the remains of a stupa and monastery built under Lalitaditya in the 8th century.

The Martand sun temple, near Anantnag, was built by Lalitaditya Muktapida in the 8th century. Its ruined central shrine stands in a large colonnaded courtyard of cusped arches and trefoil niches, the hallmarks of the Kashmir style. At Avantipora, King Avantivarman built the Avantiswami and Avantiswara temples in the 9th century, with fine carved panels. Pandrethan near Srinagar has a small, well preserved stone temple standing in water.

Kashmiri temples use pyramidal roofs in stone, copying timber construction, and pediments influenced by Gandharan and Gupta art. Our lecture on [temple superstructures](temple-superstructures.html) explains how these roofs differ from the curved Nagara towers of the plains.

sections.h2: Srinagar: wooden shrines and Mughal gardens
paras: Srinagar's Khanqah-e-Maula (Shah-e-Hamadan) and the Jamia Masjid show the valley's timber architecture, with layered wooden walls, pyramidal roofs and papier-mâché interiors. The Pathar Masjid, built under Nur Jahan, is in stone. On the slopes of Dal lake the Mughal gardens of Nishat, Shalimar and Chashme Shahi use terraces and water channels.
Hari Parbat fort, the old city's ghats and wooden bridges, and Pari Mahal complete the picture. See our [Srinagar heritage walk guide](heritage-walk-in-srinagar.html) for routes.

sections.h2: Jammu region and planning a visit
paras: In the Jammu region, Akhnoor on the Chenab is an excavated site with Harappan and later finds and Kushan-period terracottas. The Babor temples near Udhampur and the temples at Krimchi have carved stone shrines of about the 8th to 11th centuries. Jammu city has the Raghunath temple, Bahu Fort and the Mubarak Mandi palace of the Dogra rulers.

Check current travel advisories before you go. Spring and autumn suit the valley best. We build a [study tour for your group](a-study-tour-built-for-your-group.html) around Srinagar, Martand and Burzahom, with a Sharada session before travel.

faq.q: Are there UNESCO World Heritage Sites in Jammu and Kashmir?
faq.a: No. Jammu and Kashmir has no site on the UNESCO World Heritage List. Several places, including the Mughal gardens of Kashmir, have been proposed on India's tentative list.
Burzahom near Srinagar is the main Neolithic site of Kashmir. It is known for pit dwellings dug into the ground, burials with dogs, bone tools and a stone slab engraved with a hunting scene.

faq.q: Who built the Martand Sun Temple?
faq.a: The Martand Sun Temple was built by the Karkota king Lalitaditya Muktapida in the 8th century. Its ruined central shrine and colonnaded courtyard show the cusped arches and trefoil niches typical of Kashmiri temples.
Sharada is a script descended from Brahmi that was used in Kashmir from about the 8th century to write Sanskrit and Kashmiri. Many Kashmiri manuscripts and inscriptions are in Sharada.

posts.hook: Kashmir's first farmers lived in pits.
posts.caption: At Burzahom, Neolithic people dug dwellings into the ground. Later they buried dogs with their dead.

posts.hook: At Martand, walk the courtyard first.
posts.caption: The colonnade of cusped arches around the shrine is the clearest example of Kashmir's temple style. Then look at the trefoil niches.
